title: Procedures: CREATE PROCEDURE and CALL
what_is_it: A PROCEDURE is written almost exactly like a FUNCTION, but it's meant to perform actions (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) rather than compute and return a value - it has no RETURNS clause, and you invoke it with CALL as its own statement instead of using it inside a SELECT.
why_it_matters: Once a piece of business logic is really 'do these writes' rather than 'compute this value,' a procedure is the more honest fit than a function - CALL makes it clear at the call site that you're running an action, not evaluating an expression.
output:
CREATE PROCEDURE
CALL
(every Engineering employee's salary is now 500 higher)
common_mistakes: Trying to SELECT a procedure the way you would a function - that's a syntax error, since a procedure has no return value to select. Also forgetting that DROP PROCEDURE, like DROP FUNCTION, needs the full parameter-type signature, since Postgres allows the same name to exist more than once with different parameter types.
mini_exercise: Why does CREATE PROCEDURE have no RETURNS clause at all, while CREATE FUNCTION always does?
postgres_note: PROCEDURE and CALL were only added in Postgres 11 - before that version, everything (including pure side-effect logic) had to be written as a FUNCTION, even when it never returned a meaningful value.
